title: Capacity commitment & autoscale operational rhythm — Q4 planning for Dedicated pools
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Objective: Define a repeatable operational rhythm and commitment model for Dedicated GPU pools that pairs autoscale policies with reservation cadence so customers get predictable latency and unit economics while we maintain capacity efficiency. Scope: Sizing rules, commitment tiers, canary + fallback policies, billing/commit reconciliation flows, console UX for commitments and autoscale overrides, and SLAs for burst/baseline. Out of scope: changes to the underlying allocator kernels or hardware procurement process. Success metrics: 1) 30% reduction in complaint incidents tied to unexpected throttling for customers on committed plans within first quarter after rollout; 2) Reduce average cost-per-token for committed traffic by 12% vs on-demand baseline (measured by per-token chargebacks in console); 3) <5% increase in total reserved capacity utilization variance month-over-month. Risks: Under-forecasting demand at multi-tenant scale causing capacity contention; misaligned incentives (customers preferring burst mode to avoid committing); billing reconciliation edge-cases across metered and committed usage. Assumptions: Dedicated pools will continue to be provisioned as capacity groups (per-region, per-tenant options) and autoscale will operate at pool-level with tenant-level overrides. Notes about trade-offs: We can prioritize per-tenant autoscale policies (fine-grained control) but that increases control plane complexity; alternatively a pool-level policy simplifies operations but may force us into more conservative safety margins that raise cost. Proposed approach is a hybrid: pool-level autoscale for base baseline + optional per-tenant burst tokens billed at a premium.
